newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT-RUGBY UNION-Bailout saves Athletic Park test matches.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT-RUGBY UNION-Bailout saves Athletic Park test matches.

text.p: Top-level rugby will stay in Wellington after a financial rescue package to upgrade tatty Athletic Park was announced on Friday, the Evening Post newspaper reported.

Wellington liquor chain Nicholsons -- owned by the region's five licensing trusts -- has agreed to help pay for essential improvements so fans can see the All Blacks in Wellington for at least three more years.
Super 12 matches, featuring the Wellington Hurricanes, will also stay in the capital.
It is understood Nicholsons is putting up the $340,000 required to improve entrances, toilets and player facilities at the park, the paper said.

A levy on ticket sales -- $2 for a test and $1 for a Super 12 match -- will help recover some of the money. The park will be called Nicholsons Athletic Park for the next three years, said the Evening Post.

The New Zealand Rugby Football Union (NZRFU) had threatened to stop using Wellington as a test venue after many spectators missed the start of last year's Bledisloe Cup test against Australia because of the delays in getting into the park's
stands.
Union chairman Ritchie Guy described the facilities as a disgrace.
Last month the city council turned down a Wellington Rugby Union request to help fund improvements, even though top matches inject millions of dollars into the regional economy.
The NZRFU then gave the Wellington union until March 10 to come up with the $340,000.
Nicholsons said it expected a commercial return from the deal and insisted the regional economy would benefit.
It would not give specific details about the package, citing commercial sensitivity.
A delighted Wellington Rugby Football Union chairman Murray McCaw described Nicholsons as a "white knight".
Tenders had already been accepted and he hoped upgrading work would start by the end of the month. It is expected to take two and a half months to complete.
The package means New Zealand matches against Argentina this June, South Africa next year and Australia, or another top nation, in 1999 will be played in Wellington.
Wellington's planned railyard stadium is scheduled to be built after that.
McCaw said Nicholsons executives had approached the union within hours of the council's rejection.
In the past, naming rights for the park would have been unthinkable, but the Wellington board was taking a commercial and pragmatic approach.
"We need help and we have used the naming right to achieve this."
Money raised in a public appeal launched just before Christmas would still go towards the improvements though it is understood less than $1000 had been raised.
NZRFU chief executive David Moffett greeted news of the bailout with enthusiasm and said South Africa was the likely visitor to the park next year.
Wellington Mayor Mark Blumsky said rugby was important for Wellington and it was "highly appropriate that a community-owned organisation like Nicholsons has picked up the pass."
